scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In the 1970s, singer Mariza Koch revitalized these island traditions, which use microtonal string bending on the lyre and violin to navigate ancient modes like Rast and Beyati.
This is Nisiotika. 1970s (Revival) to present.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Nisiotika, meaning 'insular songs,' originated in the Aegean islands of Greece.
The tradition has been shaped by the maritime culture of the region and was significantly revived in the 1970s by artists like Mariza Koch.
It is now a global tradition, practiced in the Greek diaspora in Turkey, Australia, and the United States.

Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Nisiotika are performed at weddings, religious festivals, and social gatherings.
They serve as a vital expression of island identity and history, such as the Mihanikos which honors the sponge diving industry.
The songs often deal with themes of the sea and longing.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The tradition encompasses various dances including the Syrtos, Ballos, and Sousta.
While specific steps vary by island, they generally involve chain formations or partner pairings.
For example, the Mihanikos mimics the limping gait of a diver, while the Pidikhtos involves springing movements.
Watch for Mihanikos step.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is dominated by the lyre and violin, which are played microtonally using string bending to reach intervals in modes like Rast, Ussak, and Beyati.
Accompanying instruments include the laouto, tsampouna (bagpipe), and souravli.
Listen for the Lyre, Violin, Laouto, Tsampouna.
The pulse is Varies (2/4, 7/8, 8/8) at about 115 beats a minute.

A bright, fluid sound dominated by microtonal violin or lyre melodies over the rhythmic, percussive strumming of the laouto. The use of modes like Rast and Beyati gives it a distinct Eastern Mediterranean character.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dances are traditionally performed in village squares or during island festivals (panigiria).
While specific costumes vary by island, they often include the vraka (breeches) for men.
The setting is typically the open-air spaces of the Aegean islands, reflecting the maritime environment.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Mariza Koch, credited with the 1970s revival, and the Konitopoulos family (Giorgos, Vangelis, Eirini, Nasia, and Stella).
Other prominent musicians include Yiannis Parios, Domna Samiou, Nikos Ikonomidis, and Stathis Koukoularis.
Variants exist across the Aegean, including the Ikariotikos of Ikaria, the Lerikos of Leros, the Parianos of Paros, and the Pirgousikos of Chios.
Nisiotika is a subclass of Greek folk dance and Ionian Islands folk music.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Nisiotika is influence of Cretan music: Prominent elements of Cretan music are found in the Dodecanese and Cyclades.
Nisiotika is variant of Syrtos: A primary dance form within the Nisiotika repertoire.
Nisiotika is variant of Ballos: A partner dance often paired with Nisiotika songs.
